## Why re-test this one

By the time [RQ1](../state-decision-value/index.qmd), [RQ2/H1](../factored-vs-flat-state/index.qmd)
and [H2](../h2-calibration-retest/index.qmd) had been through the full protocol, only two of
the proposal's hypotheses had never faced it. **H8** was the one I expected to survive: it is a
claim about *constraints* rather than *forecasts*, and constraints are closer to arithmetic
than to signal.

That expectation turned out to be right in an unhelpful way. The parts that are arithmetic are
arithmetic all the way down — including the part the original counted as evidence.

## The confound

The [original experiment](../hard-risk-limits/index.qmd) took a deliberately aggressive **2×
leveraged long** and layered hard limits on it: a leverage cap at 1.5×, a volatility/CVaR
budget, and a drawdown kill-switch. The limited versions had far shallower drawdowns and
better Calmar, and the conclusion was that hard limits turn an untradeable strategy into a
viable one.

**Every one of those limits also reduces exposure.** A cap takes 2× to 1.5×. A volatility
budget scales down. A kill-switch halves. So two effects are tangled together:

**Drawdown falls because you hold less.** This is the same artefact caught in the
[RQ1 overlay](../state-decision-value/index.qmd): a rule that cuts exposure always shows a
shallower drawdown, whether or not it cuts it at useful moments.

**Calmar is not scale-invariant.** Under compounding, leverage $k$ earns roughly
$k\mu - k^2\sigma^2/2$ in log terms. Less leverage means less volatility drag, so a lower-
leverage strategy tends to a better CAGR-to-drawdown ratio *mechanically*. "Capped beats
uncapped on Calmar" is close to a statement about compounding rather than about risk
management.

## The benchmark that fixes it

Compare each limited strategy against a **constant leverage scaled to carry the same realised
volatility**. Constant exposure has no risk management in it whatsoever — no cap, no budget,
no reaction to anything. If a limit is worth having, it has to beat that.

Three indices — NAS100, US500, US30 — daily from 2015, net of 2bp on turnover, with the
benchmark charged the same entry cost so a one-day fee cannot masquerade as underperformance.
Significance by **stationary block bootstrap** (2,000 resamples, 21-day blocks), because daily
returns are serially dependent in volatility and an i.i.d. bootstrap would manufacture
significance for the same reason the forecasting tests need Newey-West.

Both **Sharpe** and **Calmar** are tested. That matters: Sharpe is a mean-variance measure and
cannot see a rule that reshapes the *tail* without changing mean-variance efficiency — which
is precisely what a drawdown control is supposed to do.

![Left: mean maximum drawdown across the three indices. Against an unconstrained 2× (pale bars) every limit looks transformative. Against constant leverage carrying the same risk (darker bars), the limited strategy — the blue dot — sits almost exactly on top of the benchmark for the leverage cap and the kill-switch, and below it only for the volatility budget. Right: the Calmar gap against matched risk, per limit and index. Only the volatility budget is consistently positive, and no comparison is significant.](fig-h8-retest.png){fig-alt="Maximum drawdown for three limits against two benchmarks, and Calmar gaps versus matched-risk constant leverage."}

## Results

**The leverage cap does exactly nothing — and that is not a figure of speech.**

| | Sharpe gap | Calmar gap | p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| NAS100 | −0.000 | 0.000 | 1.00 |
| US500 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 1.00 |
| US30 | −0.000 | −0.000 | 1.00 |

A constant leverage cap *is* constant leverage. Once the benchmark is constant leverage at the
same volatility, the two strategies are the same strategy and there is nothing left to
measure. The entire apparent benefit in the original is the arithmetic of holding less.

Finding that required fixing a bug in my own test: when two return streams are identical the
bootstrap has zero variance, and floating-point noise was reading as p = 0.010. The test now
detects the degenerate case and reports p = 1.00.

**The kill-switch is consistently worse.** Sharpe gaps of −0.068, −0.069 and −0.057; Calmar
negative on all three. Directionally this confirms the original's own finding that reactive
drawdown rules backfire — selling after the fall and buying back after the recovery.

**The volatility budget is the one that might be real.** It is positive on all three assets on
*both* metrics — six for six in sign:

| | Sharpe gap | Calmar gap | p (Calmar) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| NAS100 | +0.099 | **+0.173** | 0.26 |
| US500 | +0.060 | **+0.206** | 0.19 |
| US30 | +0.051 | **+0.155** | 0.29 |

The Calmar gains are large in relative terms — a mean of +0.178 against a matched-risk Calmar
of roughly 0.30, so about **+60%**. And the pattern is exactly what a risk control should look
like: a big improvement in drawdown-per-unit-of-return with only a small change in Sharpe,
meaning it is reshaping the tail rather than improving mean-variance efficiency.

**But nothing is significant. Zero of nine comparisons on Sharpe, zero of nine on Calmar.**

## The verdict — H8 does not survive, with one live thread

**H8 as stated is not supported.** Against a benchmark carrying the same risk, hard limits do
not demonstrably improve viability. One of the three does nothing at all by construction, one
is consistently harmful, and the third is consistently helpful but never distinguishable from
noise on three correlated indices.

**The volatility budget deserves a proper test rather than a verdict.** Six-for-six in sign
with a ~60% relative Calmar gain is the most promising unfalsified result anywhere in this lab.
It is also exactly the signature that has repeatedly failed to survive widening — `ewma_slope`
was 7 for 7 in sign and cleared the bar on 2 of 7 assets; the H2 residual was 3 for 3 and
cleared nothing. Consistent-but-never-significant has been this lab's most reliable false
positive.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**This completes the audit, and the result is uncomfortable.** Every hypothesis that has now
faced the full protocol — RQ1, RQ2/H1, H5, H2 and H8 — has returned a null or a near-null. Only
**H6** (benefit concentrating at transitions) remains untested. The proposal's empirical
position is that its architecture is not yet supported by its own evidence, and the honest
thing is to say so rather than to keep the earlier verdicts on the page.
:::

## Limitations

- **Not an exact replication.** The original used a 2016 out-of-sample start and different
  budget parameters; this uses 2015 and the harness's own settings, so the absolute drawdowns
  differ from the published −63% → −26%. It tests *the same claim under a fair benchmark*, not
  the same code.
- **Three correlated indices.** Nine comparisons are nowhere near nine independent tests. With
  a deflated bar this would be harder still, so "0 of 9" is already generous.
- **One matched-risk definition.** Matching on realised volatility is the natural choice, but
  matching on average exposure or on ex-ante volatility would give slightly different
  benchmarks.
- **The volatility budget is under-powered here, not disproven.** Three assets cannot resolve a
  Calmar gap of this size at p < 0.05. A seven-asset test is the obvious next step and the one
  I would run before drawing any conclusion about it.
- **Costs are simple.** 2bp on turnover, no slippage model, no financing cost on leverage —
  and financing would hurt the higher-exposure strategies most, so the comparison is if
  anything generous to the unconstrained base.

## What I learned

**A constraint that is a constant is not a constraint.** The leverage cap result is the
cleanest thing in this entry: comparing "2× capped at 1.5×" against "2× uncapped" tells you
about 1.5× versus 2×, which you already knew. The only informative comparison is against
something carrying the same risk, and once you build it the cap has nothing to say.

The wider lesson is the one this lab has now learned four separate ways: **the benchmark is
where the result lives.** Raw drawdown versus an unconstrained base, a tercile rule versus a
filtered HMM, own-span scoring versus a common window, a rich model versus a small one — each
time the treatment was fine and the comparison was doing the work. Effect sizes get
scrutinised. Benchmarks mostly do not.

::: {.status-note}

long, net 2bp on turnover. Limits: leverage cap 1.5×; volatility budget ≈17.5% annualised via
`min(2, budget/rv20)`; drawdown kill-switch halving exposure after a −20% trailing drawdown.
Benchmark: constant leverage $m$ set so realised volatility matches the limited strategy's,
charged the same day-one entry cost. Significance: stationary block bootstrap, 2,000 resamples,
21-day blocks, on both Sharpe and Calmar differences, with a degeneracy guard for the case
where the two return streams coincide. Results: leverage cap gap exactly 0.000 on all three
assets (p = 1.00); kill-switch Sharpe −0.068 / −0.069 / −0.057; volatility budget Sharpe
+0.099 / +0.060 / +0.051 and Calmar +0.173 / +0.206 / +0.155 (p = 0.26 / 0.19 / 0.29).
